I was a house guard in the hall of a minor lord near Emyn Beraid. He paid little and I gave most of it away, to the widows of the garrison and the families of rangers who did not come back. A guard's work is quiet, and I liked that mine was useful.

A raid by the goblins of Blue Craig burned the hall one winter night. The lord died on the stair and I carried his steward's children out. The survivors of the village, nearly forty, followed me to Fornost, where the king's stewards found them a corner of a warehouse and little else.
I stay with them when I can and send what I earn, which is never enough. A guard with no hall is a guard for hire, and I will take any honest wage that feeds them.
Looking after the survivors is as worthy as any battle.
You cannot keep forty people alive with one sword and no pay.
If you can pay a fair wage and spare a ration for my people, I will serve you faithfully.
Guards of the minor lords' halls near Emyn Beraid earn little and keep the village widows fed. When a hall burns, the survivors turn to us.
Have you a moment? The families at the south gate need someone to speak for them...

I was a junior clerk to the king's stewards at Fornost Erain, tallying grain and writing letters for lords who could not write their own. I was good with people, and the old clerks sent me to talk to the angry ones. I came to like it.

When families fleeing the burned villages of the North Downs reached the capital by the hundreds, a clan lord argued the gates should close to save the stores. I wrote down their names, kept a ledger of who was sick and who was starving, and put it before the council. They called it sentiment and had me removed from my post.

I learned that a ledger can be a plea if you write it well. Now I go from town to town gathering food, coin and sworn blades for those families. The North is poor, but there is more kindness in it than anyone admits.
Names on a page can save lives, and you wrote them.
The council was right to count the stores before the sentiment.
Take me with you, and I will find you provisions, goodwill and honest allies.
Fornost's stewards keep the counts of grain and refugees. A few of us have spoken up for the North Downs folk and been sent away for it.
The road from Dale to the lake is longer than it looks, friend.

I rode the post between Dale and Esgaroth, carrying letters, coin and now and then a sick child to the healer. Every rider on that road knew me, and I knew every ford and farm along the River Running.

One autumn the grain wagon I was guarding came upon a village burned out by raiders from Rhun. I gave the families half the load without asking leave. The guild factor called it theft and wrote my name in his ledger.
No guild will hire a man marked for that, so I ride for whoever pays, and I still stop at every farm on the way. I cannot seem to help it. My horse is all that is left of that life.
Feeding the hungry is no crime to me.
A rider who gives away other men's grain is a poor courier.
Trust me with a message, a purse or a wounded man, and I will carry it anywhere you point.
Riders of the Dale road know every ford between the Mountain and the lake. We go wherever the roads still need carrying.
My name is older than my fortune. Have you heard of the house of Girion?
My family claims kinship with Girion, the last Lord of Dale before the dragon came, so I was taught young to lead men and to sit a horse. I rose to command thirty spears on the eastern road.

I held a ford on the River Running with thirty spears when a larger band came through from the east. My captain withdrew in the night and left us the order to hold. I held it, and eleven men died before help arrived.

The council praised the ford and then quietly passed me over for every command, because I had named my captain's flight aloud. I carry the eleven names with me. A man who will not lie for his betters finds few doors open.
You did what honor asked of you.
Perhaps your captain saw the field better than you did.
If you need someone to hold a line and keep faith with the men in it, I will lead a company for you.
The sons of Dale's old houses are raised to lead men and to ride out when the horns sound. Some of us find our commands elsewhere.
Looking for someone who knows the roads. I do.
I scouted for the merchant caravans that run from Dale to the Iron Hills and the gates of Erebor. Water, ambush ground, safe fords, I priced them all. A good scout is paid by the mile.

When the Easterling raids went quiet, the caravan master tried to cut my wage and said there was no danger left to pay for. Quiet was my work. I took my maps and left him to find his own way, and two carts were lost that season.
No factor trusts me now, and I trust none of them back. I carry my own pay and I count it twice.
A man should be paid for his craft.
You left honest drivers to the raiders.
Pay me on time and I will put you on the best ground between here and the Mountain.
Caravan scouts of Dale sell the roads they know to anyone who pays on time. We are not sentimental about it.
A man of Lake-town on dry land. Try not to laugh, I have heard it all.

I walked the boardwalks of Esgaroth with the town watch, a boat-spear in my hands, keeping thieves out of the fish stalls. Hold a long spear on a rocking deck for ten years and you can use it anywhere.

I noticed the Master's toll-men taking more silver than they ever wrote down. I kept my own tally and took it to the council, and I was struck from the watch rolls before the ink dried. The week before, I had let a starving boy go, so I was blamed for that too.
So here I am, a watchman without a town, holding a ledger nobody wants. I keep the tally anyway, in case a better council ever asks.
Counting honestly should never cost a man his post.
A watchman who frees thieves has himself to blame.
I can hold a spear steady on any ground, and I can read your quartermaster's books, for a fair share.
I learned the long spear on the pitching decks of Lake-town's watch. Few things steady the hand like that.
The lads named me after the dragon-slayer. I have not earned it yet, but I will.

My father told the tale of the dragon's fall every night of my childhood. The other boys named me after the dragon-slayer as a joke because I would not stop asking for more of it. At sixteen I took a spear from the Dale armory and swore to make the joke true.
Word came of raiders from Rhun near our hills, and I led six lads out to meet them without waiting for the garrison. I never counted the enemy, and there were forty. Three of the six came home.
The garrison does not trust me with a command now, and my father will not speak of it. I would sooner die useful than live as a joke. I still carry the spear.
Courage learns from its mistakes.
You threw boys at forty men for the sake of a nickname.
Let me stand in your front rank, and I will earn what the lads called me or learn I never could.
Young spearmen of Dale grow up on the story of the dragon's fall. Some of us go looking for a fight that big.
Forgive me, I only wished to see a friendly face.

My father fished the Long Lake and I fished it after him, hauling nets at dawn and mending them at dusk. When the watch needed spears, I took up the boat-hook and a place in the line, being strong and no worse than most.
When a raiding band came across the ice one winter, I froze. The lads on either side of me did not. Two never came back, and I was crouched behind a woodpile when they fell.
I do not blame the cold, for I know what I did. Since then I give away what coin I earn to the widows of Esgaroth, and it is never enough.
Fear touches every man. You have paid for it.
A man who breaks from the line is no use to me.
If you can use a man who knows his own failing, I will carry a spear for you and try to stand firmer than I did.
Fishermen of the Long Lake take up the boat-hook and the spear when the watch calls. Not all of us stand when the shouting starts.
You carry a bow? Good. Then you will understand.
I was the best archer in Dale at twenty, with a black-fletched arrow on my quiver in honor of Bard. The great shoot at the midsummer fair was mine to lose, and I wanted it badly.

A rival from Esgaroth shot as well as I did, so the night before the final I cut his string a third of the way through. He drew at the line and it snapped across his cheek. They found the cut ends in my pack.

I was stripped of my fletching and barred from the butts. I still shoot better than any man in the hall, and they know it, and it changes nothing. I am not sorry I wanted to win, only that I was caught.
Skill like yours should not rot unused.
A man who cuts his rival's string deserves the ban.
Take me on and I will put an arrow wherever you point. Do not ask me for more than that.
Archers of Dale are raised on Bard's legend and shoot at the butts every feast day. Some of us carry the bow wherever the pay is fair.
Nothing watches a road like an old rider with a good horse.

My father was a boy when the dragon fell, and I grew up watching Dale rebuilt stone by stone. I rode the Ravenhill post for twenty years, carrying word between the old watch above the city and the gates.

One spring the ravens brought news of an Easterling muster in the east, and I rode to the council with it. The lord called ravens gossip and kept me waiting three weeks. By the time he believed it, the villages on the eastern fells had burned.
I kept my honor and lost my post, since the lord could not forgive having been wrong. Now I ride where a warning is still welcome. It is a short list.
You were right, and they should have listened.
Ravens bring rumor. A sensible lord waits for proof.
I know the eastern roads and the minds of men who ignore warnings. I will ride ahead for you.
I come from the Ravenhill riders, who watch the eastern roads for Dale. A warning from us is sound, whatever the lords choose to do with it.
Hard country makes hard men. Do not expect me to apologize.

I served as a sergeant on the Iron Hills road, where Dale's spearmen stand beside the dwarves against whatever comes down from the north. The dwarves taught me to keep the spear steady and the line closed, and to waste nothing, pity included.

We took a band of Easterling raiders who had burned three farms, and I put the prisoners down rather than march them for days to the stocks. My captain called it murder. The dwarves said nothing, which I took for agreement.
I was dismissed with no pay owed and no word to carry. I would do it again. The farms along that road stayed safe the rest of the year.
Hard choices keep the roads safe.
Killing prisoners is plain murder.
I fight hard and I do not flinch. If that suits you, put me at the front of your line.
Dale's spearmen hold the Iron Hills road beside the dwarves, and the work there is not gentle. We learn it, and we do not forget it.
Have you heard whether the eastern fells are quiet this season?

I bred and broke horses on the fells east of the Lonely Mountain, where the grass is thin and the horses are hardy. I rode before I could properly walk, and half the mounts in the valley carry my training.

Raiders from Rhun came at harvest and drove off our herd and half our village. I rode to Dale for help, but the council would not hear me before morning, so I gathered the farmhands and went after them myself.

We took back most of the horses and every child, but two farmhands did not return, and the village is a burned ring of posts. I sold the herd to pay the dead men's families. A rider's hands are all I have left.
You gave everything you had. That counts.
A hothead who rides off without leave gets men killed.
I will ride for you gladly, and I will give my last coin to anyone you want to help.
Horse-breeders of the eastern fells raise sturdy mounts and riders who ask little. We are quick to the saddle when the raiders come.
Walls fall to whoever knows where they are weak. I know.

I raised siege towers and rams for a war-chief of the high plains, cutting timber that we Variags had never bothered to use. When the chief's host marched on a Haradrim border fortress, my engines went with it, and its walls shook under them.
After the siege he paid me in captives I had no use for and a lame horse. So I sold the plans and two spare rams to a rival clan, and the chief put a price on my head that his riders still chase.
I own a mallet, a bad name and a map of every ford between here and the Ash Mountains. The dead in those pens never troubled my sleep, but the debt of an unpaid wage does.
A man who can break walls is worth more than a man who only climbs them.
You cheated your own chief. Why would I be safe from you?
Give me timber and a few hands, and I will build you something that opens any gate.
I am a siege-builder out of the Variag clans, and I go where the walls are thick and the pay is thicker.
I swore my blade once. I would swear it again, if the man were worth it.
I was sworn blade-brother to the heir of a horse clan, and we rode together from boyhood. I won my place in the war-band with the sword, against older men, and never lost a duel I was given.

The heir ordered a surrendered caravan guard put to the axe, and I stepped between them. He struck me across the face, and his clan named me oath-breaker, which in Khand is worse than being named dead.
I carry my sword, my scar and the shame of a vow that bound me to a butcher. I have no clan, no camp, and no one left who will share a fire with me.
Keeping faith with the helpless is no shame. The shame was his.
An oath is an oath. You broke yours, whatever your reasons.
Name me a cause I can serve without lowering my sword, and I will follow you to the end of it.
I am a Variag swordsman who served a clan chief's household, and I fight best at the front of a charge.
I have watched this country for thirty years. Ask me anything about the plains and I will tell you who is riding across them.

I was a horse-archer and scout for the caravans that cross the plains of Khand toward the southern roads. I knew every well, every ambush hollow, and which Haradrim raiders took coin to look the other way.
One season the chief who hired me sold our route to the very raiders we guarded against. I warned the caravan masters and shot two of his men for it, and he had me dismissed before the rains came.
Now I ride alone, with a bow, a good eye, and a name the caravan masters speak quietly. Honest guards are rare, and the chiefs who pay them are rarer.
A man who keeps his word to those who hire him is worth more than any chief's gold.
You killed your own side's men. Do not expect me to praise that.
If you need eyes ahead of your column and a shaft that finds its mark, I will ride scout for you.
I am a plains scout and horse-archer who walked the caravan roads between Khand and the southern markets.
Come closer, I do not bite. Not unless the wound is already festering.

I learned the cutting trade as a boy in a Variag war-camp, holding lamps while the camp surgeon sewed up men who had lost bets with an axe. By twenty I could set a bone, burn out a rot, and curse a fever faster than anyone south of the Ash Mountains.

I gave away the chief's wound-wine and bandages to anyone who asked, even a captured Haradrim scout, and the chief took the strap to my back for wasting his stores on the enemy. I did not stay to see what he planned next.
I still carry a kit of needles, a bottle of spirits, and a conscience nobody warned me about. I keep patching people and still wonder why it never pays.
You mended what the chiefs break. That counts for more than the stores you spent.
Free medicine for the enemy is just a fancy way to arm him.
I will sew up your wounded and your enemies too, if you can stand the sight of it.
I am a camp surgeon from the Variag war-hosts, patching up axe wounds and arrow cuts for anyone with coin or kindness.
Every road has a price. I know the price of most.

I was a factor for the slave caravans that ran from the markets of Khand south to the Harad coast. I kept the ledgers, bribed the toll-keepers, and bought and sold more men and horses than I could count.
A partner I trusted sold the whole convoy to Easterling buyers while I slept, and I was left in the dust with the ledgers and an empty purse. The cargo I did not mourn, but the silver I did.
I have nothing but a head for sums and a long list of men who owe me. I intend to collect from every one of them before I die.
A man who can make a profit from nothing is useful to any cause.
You sold men. I will not forget it, however polite you are.
Put me in charge of your coin and your caravans, and you will see a profit within a season.
I am a caravan factor out of the Khand markets, and I know how silver moves between the plains and the south.
You have the look of someone with something worth taking. Relax, I only admire.
I grew up in the shadow of a war-camp, picking pockets among the warriors and fencing what they plundered. By the time I was grown, I could empty a chief's tent without waking the dogs.
I robbed a clan's war-chest, and when the riders closed in, I gave them the names of my whole gang to save my own neck. I do not pretend it was brave, only that it worked.
I have a few coins, a sharp blade and a talent for slipping out of trouble that I should not be proud of. I am, and the clans never forget a face.
A clever thief knows when to run. You lived to tell it.
You sold out your own people. I should check my purse.
Take me on, and I will find you what your enemies hide, and keep my hands to myself, mostly.
I am a camp thief and fence out of the Variag war-camps, and I know every back way into a chief's tent.
I led forty riders at nineteen. I would have led four hundred, given the chance.

I took command of a war-band of the plains when its captain died at a ford, and I won my first fight with a feint that drew a Haradrim column into a gully. By the next summer the riders called me by a title I had not earned yet.

I kept the plunder for myself and paid my men in promises, and the promises ran out before the winter did. Half of them deserted at the next camp, and the rest followed me like ghosts until I let them go.
I have a sword, a good horse, and a lesson I have only half learned about what men follow. I do not intend to lose a second command.
A leader learns more from one loss than from ten wins.
You cheated men who bled for you. A fool commands that way.
Give me riders and a plan, and I will teach you what a Variag feint does to a line.
I am a young war-band captain of the Variag riders, trained to read a field and break a line.
You want an axe that will not shatter at the first blow? Good. Most do not know to ask.
I forged weapons in a Khand camp for twenty years, the curved cutting axes that my people are known for, balanced and hungry. Every blade I made, I tested on a post of iron oak before I sold it.

The chief ordered me to forge collars and chains for his slave caravans, and I refused, though he offered twice the silver. He burned my forge to the ground, with the tools my father left me inside it.
I walk with a hammer, a scarred hand, and a stubborn pride that cost me everything. I never regretted it, and I suspect I never will.
A craftsman who refuses to make chains still makes the world better.
You could have made the collars and lived richly. Pride is a poor trade.
Set me up with a forge and iron, and I will arm your people better than any smith in the south.
I am an axe-smith out of the Khand camps, and I can make a blade to bite through helm and bone alike.
There is no creature in the world I understand better than a horse. People are harder.

I was a horse-breaker and lancer in a clan whose wealth stood in its herds. I broke wild colts from the plains, rode the ridge-line at dawn, and charged at the head of the lances when the clan went to war.

In a feud raid, I found a wounded boy of the rival clan hiding in a gully, and I lifted him onto my horse and carried him to his own people's tents. My clan called it treason, and my own chief had my herd driven off.
I have one horse left, the colt I could not bear to part with, and a saddle that is still mine. The plains still call me, but no clan will receive me.
You showed mercy when mercy was all you had. That is not treason.
You helped the enemy's child. Your clan was right to be angry.
Give me a horse under me and a lance, and I will carry your banner ahead of every charge.
I am a horse-breaker and lancer from the plains clans, raised in the saddle among the herds of Khand.
I will be honest with you. I am not brave, but I am very hard to hit.

I trained as an archer in a Variag battle line, loosing from the rear while the axemen held the front. I could put an arrow through a mailed throat at two hundred paces, and I took pride in the number I kept in my quiver.

When the line broke in a border war against the Haradrim, I shot until the horns blew, then dropped my bow and ran. Better to live as a coward than to die as a corpse, I told myself, and I have told myself that every night since.
I am a deserter now, with a price on me in the war-camps and a sharp bow I never learned to stop using. Fear has made me careful, and I am still alive.
Running from a lost fight is not the same as cowardice. You kept your arm.
You left your comrades to die. I do not trust that kind of nerve.
Keep me behind your line with a bow and a clear target, and I will be worth every coin.
I am an archer from the Variag battle lines, trained to shoot from behind the axes and stay alive.
